the central integration and resolution of rotational and gravitational vestibular signals is abnormal in migraine and vestibular migraine, but not in vestibular neuritis.

the brain normally uses a complex and dynamic set of mechanisms to minimize the sensory conflict between canal and otolith cues and that this conflict is increased in VM patients, which may be a key factor in the enhanced motion intolerance and episody vertigo that characterize VM.
the brain normally integrates the information from the vestibular organs in an adaptive manner to reduce intravestibulo-ocular sensory conflict.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

VM patients have an abnormality in the central integration of canal and otolith cues that results in an enhanced conflict between these signals and that this abnormality may be responsible for some of the symptoms that characterize VM.

migraine patients, but not VM subjects, are capable of normal conflict resolution, which may explain the enhanced motion sickness susceptibility in migraine, but VM patients have a deficit in conflict resolution, which explains their motion sickness and vertigo symptoms.

VM is a disorder of central vestibular processing that is distinct from migraine, and that this disorder may be related to the enhanced motion intolerance and episodically impaired balance and spatial orientation that characterize this disorder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found an abnormality in the way the brain processes information about head motion in migraine and vestibular migraine patients.

the brain normally adjusts the dynamic and spatial properties of the central vestibular signals in a way to minimize the intravestibulo-ocular sensory conflict and this process is disrupted during migraine.
we have identified the first objective biomarker of vestibular migraine, which can be measured in the clinic and used to objectively assess treatment outcomes.
